lines.name: Level: B1+ · Topic: The Newspaper Office

lines.text:
Extra! Extra! — A Morning at the Newspaper Office

The newsroom at the Daily Herald is already busy at seven in the morning. Reporters sit at computer terminals, typing articles before the deadline. A telephone rings every few minutes. Coffee cups cover every desk. The wall clock reminds everyone that time is running out.

At the centre of the room, the editor sits at her desk, reading the morning's draft articles on her screen. A whiteboard behind her lists the day's stories. A pinboard displays photographs, maps, and interview notes. She must decide which story goes on the front page and write the headline — the large, bold title that makes people want to read more.

Each person in the newsroom has a different role. A reporter goes out to find news, carrying a notebook, a pen, a voice recorder, and a press pass. A photographer takes pictures to go with the articles. Each photograph needs a caption — a short sentence explaining what the picture shows. A columnist writes a regular column giving their personal opinion. A copy editor checks every article for spelling and grammar mistakes before it goes to print. A proofreader does a final check on the proof — the last version before printing.

The newspaper has many different sections. The front page carries the most important stories — often breaking news that happened overnight. Inside, there are feature stories (longer, more detailed articles), opinion pieces, reviews of books or films, an editorial written by the editor, sports scores, a weather report, interviews with interesting people, investigation reports, classified ads, and obituaries.

A correspondent reports from another city or country. An intern — usually a young journalism student — helps with small tasks and learns the job. A cartoonist draws funny pictures about the news.

Once the layout is finished, the pages go to the printing press. Ink rolls across huge paper rolls, and the folding machine folds each newspaper. By early morning, a delivery truck takes the newspapers to every newsstand in the city.

In today's world, many people read news on their phones. But the skills of journalism — asking questions, checking facts, meeting deadlines, writing clearly — are the same whether the article appears on paper or on a screen.

lines.text: British newspapers are traditionally divided into broadsheets ('quality' papers like The Guardian, The Times, The Telegraph) and tabloids ('popular' papers like The Sun, the Daily Mail). Broadsheets cover politics, economics, and international affairs in depth, while tabloids focus on celebrity news, sport, and human interest stories. The distinction is cultural, not just about paper size.

lines.text: The media is sometimes called 'the fourth estate' — an informal but powerful pillar of democracy alongside the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. A free press acts as a watchdog, holding governments and institutions accountable. The World Press Freedom Index ranks countries by how freely journalists can work.

lines.text: Newspaper headlines follow special grammar rules: present simple for past events ('PM Resigns'), infinitive for future ('Mayor to Open New Hospital'), and articles are dropped ('Man Found in River'). Understanding headline language is a specific B1+ reading skill tested in Cambridge exams.

lines.text: The term 'fake news' entered mainstream vocabulary around 2016. Media literacy — the ability to critically evaluate news sources, recognise bias, and distinguish fact from opinion — is now taught in schools across Europe. The BBC's 'Reality Check' and Full Fact are examples of fact-checking services.

lines.text: 'News' is uncountable — no 'a/an' and no plural. Use 'an article', 'a story', 'a piece of news', or 'a report' when talking about one item. 'The news is good today.' 'I read two articles in the newspaper.'

lines.text: 'As' describes a role or job: 'She works as a reporter.' 'Like' means 'similar to': 'She works like a reporter' (she's not actually a reporter but works in a similar way). This difference is important: 'as a teacher' = she IS a teacher; 'like a teacher' = she acts similar to one.

lines.text: We 'do', 'conduct', or 'carry out' an interview — not 'make' an interview. Common collocations: 'do an interview', 'write an article', 'take a photograph', 'meet a deadline.' Learning these word partnerships helps your English sound natural.

lines.text: 'Say' + (to someone) + that: 'He said (to me) that...' 'Tell' + person + that: 'He told me that...' Never 'said me' or 'told to me.' 'Say' focuses on the words; 'tell' focuses on the listener.

lines.text: When something started in the past and continues now, use present perfect: 'has been published since 1952.' 'Since' + point in time always needs present perfect (simple or continuous). 'The paper has been running since 1952.' 'She has worked here since March.'
